title: Same Letter Tiles
story: You are playing a word game with letter tiles. You lay down listen. Your friend scoops up your six tiles, shuffles them, and lays down silent. Legal move: same tiles, new order.
Next round she tries to turn your teeth into teethe. That needs a sixth tile she does not have. You want a quick way to check any claimed rearrangement.
task: Write sameTiles(word, rearranged). Return true if rearranged uses exactly the same letters as word, each letter the same number of times, in any order. Otherwise return false.
Both strings contain only lowercase letters a to z. Two empty strings count as the same tiles.

examples.explanation: Both have one each of e, i, l, n, s, t. The order is different, the tiles are the same.
The lengths differ, 5 against 6, so at least one tile is missing. No need to look further.
b, r, a, g in both. Shuffled, but nothing added and nothing left over.

hints: Compare aab and abb. They use the same set of letters. Why are they still not the same tiles?
What matters is how many of each letter there are. Two words are the same tiles exactly when every letter has the same count in both.
Count the letters of the first word. How could the second word "use up" those counts, and what would you look for at the end?

If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise build a map letter → count from word, then walk rearranged and subtract one per letter. If any count drops below zero, a tile is missing: return false. If you finish, return true.
bruteForce: For each letter of word, search rearranged for a matching unused tile and cross it off. If you ever fail to find one, the answer is no.

Each search scans the second word, so this is O(n²). With 50,000 letters that is over a billion steps. Sorting both words and comparing them works in O(n log n), which is fine, but counting is simpler and faster.

walkthrough: Order does not matter, only how many of each letter there are. So count the tiles of the first word, then let the second word spend them.
• No count went below zero, so every tile was matched. Return true.
Why is it enough to check for negatives? The lengths are equal. If some letter were short, another letter would have to be over-used to make up the length, and that one would go negative.
solution.timeWhy: Two passes over strings of length n, with O(1) map work per letter.
solution.spaceWhy: The map holds at most 26 letters, however long the words are.
solution.takeaway: When order does not matter but amounts do, compare counts, not sequences. A count map (or an array of 26 counters) is the standard fingerprint for "same items, any order".
